source_title: Sideshow operators offer cash discounts for rides amid soaring costs
source_excerpt:
Bradley and Coralie Girdler set up a sideshow at the 165th Mount Gambier Spring Show. ( ABC South East SA: Josh Brine )
Country shows across are facing mounting cost challenges.
A sideshow operator says costs have risen between 30 and 50 per cent since the COVID pandemic.
Mount Gambier A&H Society show vice-president Ollie Abblitt says organisers try to find the right balance of attractions without being "too hard" on budgets.
A near doubling of the costs to run popular show rides has seen operators offering cash discounts to lure showgoers back to their favourite attractions this spring show season across southern Australia.
Showman's Guild of South Australia president Daryl Girdler said costs in his industry including fuel, insurance and wages had risen 30 to 50 per cent since the COVID pandemic.
Show ride operators are offering cash discounts for showgoers to help alleviate budget pressures. ( ABC South East SA: Josh Brine )
"But our customers are also having to deal with their own cost pressures, including interest rate rises, fuel and groceries … there's a lot of pressure on families."
Mr Girdler said sideshow and ride operators had started offering discounts for cash payments to try to help customers.
"Or they'll run out of money too quick, so we're very mindful of the fact we've got to offer good, safe, affordable family fun."
As spring show season rolls out across country South Australia and Victoria, showgoers and sideshow operators are aware of just how fragile the entertainment dollar can be.
Ticket prices for rides range from about $10 to $30, which has led to some backlash online on community forums.
Sideshow alley will feature new ride The Joker. ( ABC South East SA: Josh Brine )
Mr Girdler said the newest ride, the Joker — deemed "Australia's scariest show ride" — was a $3 million investment, requiring a fleet of three prime movers to transport and multiple generators to run.
In South Australia's south-east, Mount Gambier A&H Society show vice-president Ollie Abblitt said bringing thrill rides to regional audiences was important.
"Ultimately, costs have been on the up for everyone in recent years, but we just hope people will come and support the country shows and the people who make a living providing this entertainment."
Mr Girdler is on the road 10 months of the year with other members of his family, who are trying to carry on a multi-generation entertainment business spanning nearly a century amid the cost-of-living crisis.
"My grandfather started just after the second world war. He'd lived through the First World War, the Great Depression, and there wasn't much entertainment for people … especially out in the country."
The Girdler family have travelled to country shows across South Australia and Victoria, including the Melrose Show in 1938. ( State Library of South Australia )
In the early days, travelling across South Australia and rural Victoria by train, the Girdler family would set up their coconut shy, merry-go-round and pop gun attractions on railway sidings.
"It was a much simpler time, there was no television, no internet or phones and the people really needed cheering up," Mr Girdler said.
The Girdler family's offerings evolved from games to tent shows with Samson the Strongman, the Tattooed Lady, boxing troupes and, eventually, show rides.
"When I was a kid, it was our lifestyle," Mr Girdler recalled.
Coralie Girdler with two of her kewpie dolls, which she has made to the delight of children and showgoers since she was 15. ( Josh Brine / ABC South East )
"We'd arrive at the next show, set up our tents and gather around the campfire with other carnival folk, singing songs or listening to someone playing a guitar."
Regulation swept through the industry in the 1970s and 1980s and "cleaned out a lot of the cowboys", Mr Girdler said.
